records.place: Paarl, on the banks of the Berg River, Paarl district, Coastal Region

wine.name: Private Bin Edelkeur
wine.classification: Noble Late Harvest, the Cape's legal category for botrytised sweet wine
wine.grapes: Chenin Blanc, all of it, picked shrivelled with noble rot.
wine.sites: Botrytised blocks chosen each year from across the Western Cape: Paarl and Durbanville in some vintages, old bush vines near Darling in others; the vineyards move with where the rot takes hold.
wine.making: The botrytised Chenin is fermented cool in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks for some weeks, and the ferment is stopped when the sugar and the acidity stand in balance. In the vintages read the wine sees no wood, so the fruit and the rot speak without oak.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, honey and marmalade over quince, melon and a waxy, saffron edge of botrytis; very sweet and dense, held up by a cutting thread of Chenin acidity and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its fruit, it gains notes of tea, nuts and barley sugar over decades, and bottles of the 1970s have been sold at the auction.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white or dessert wine glass, poured in small measures.

label.means: Afrikaans for noble choice, the house's name for its botrytised Chenin.
The house's mark for wines made to be sold at its auction rather than in shops.
The legal category for sweet wine from botrytised grapes, made possible by the change in the law Edelkeur brought about.

records.table: Nederburg's Edelkeur, first made in 1969, was the Cape's first wine of nobly rotten grapes: pure Chenin Blanc, fermented cool in steel and stopped sweet. It tastes of dried apricot and honey with a bright edge, so pour it cold and in small glasses.
records.story: Philippus Wolvaart was granted the farm on the Berg River at Paarl in 1791 and named it for Sebastiaan Cornelis Nederburgh, a commissioner of the Dutch East India Company; his thatched Cape Dutch manor house, its gable dated 1800, is a national monument. The farm passed through several hands until 1937, when a German brewer who had been part owner of a brewery in Bremen bought it and set it on the path of modern winemaking, with cool, controlled fermentation. In 1956 he brought in a young German cellar master trained at Weinsberg, who stayed until 1989. In 1969 that cellar master made the Cape's first wine of grapes touched by noble rot and called it Edelkeur. Its sugar broke the law of the day, which capped unfortified wine at a low level of residual sugar, so it could not be sold. A second vintage followed only in 1972, and the compromise reached with the authorities let it be sold at auction to invited licensed traders alone. So the Nederburg Auction was born: the first, with six taking part, was held at the estate in 1975, and in 2019 it became the Cape Fine and Rare Wine Auction. The law was later changed to admit the new style. Edelkeur gave the Cape its sweet wine category and its fine wine auction at once.

others.name: The Winemasters Noble Late Harvest
others.note: The house's botrytised sweet wine for the shops, a wider bottling than the auction's Edelkeur.

others.name: Private Bin Eminence
others.note: Another sweet wine of the Private Bin range, made for the auction.

others.name: Private Bin R163 Cabernet Sauvignon

traps: Edelkeur is a Noble Late Harvest of botrytised Chenin Blanc, not a fortified Muscadel and not an unfortified Muscat like Vin de Constance.
The Nederburg Auction became the Cape Fine and Rare Wine Auction in 2019 and moved from the estate to Stellenbosch; the auction was born of Edelkeur.
Edelkeur carries Wine of Origin Western Cape in the vintages read, since its botrytised blocks are drawn from across the province, not from Paarl alone.

cards.front: Why could Nederburg's first Edelkeur of 1969 not be sold in shops?
cards.back: Its residual sugar broke the law of the day for unfortified wine, so a compromise allowed it to be sold only at auction to licensed traders.

cards.front: Which grape and which rot make Edelkeur?
cards.back: Chenin Blanc, shrivelled by botrytis cinerea, noble rot.

questions.q: A guest asks how Nederburg's Edelkeur is made. Which method fits?
opts: Botrytised Chenin fermented cool in steel and stopped sweet
Muscat fortified with grape spirit before fermentation ends
Chenin dried on straw mats, then aged in old casks
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed at dawn
questions.exp: Edelkeur is pure botrytised Chenin Blanc, fermented cool in stainless steel and stopped when sugar and acid balance; fortified Muscat is the Cape's Muscadel, a different wine.

questions.q: What did the compromise over Nederburg's first Edelkeur give the Cape wine trade?
opts: The Nederburg Auction, first held in 1975
The Wine of Origin scheme of 1973
The KWV's sole right to export surplus
The first Cap Classique sparkling wine
questions.exp: Edelkeur could be sold only at auction to invited licensed traders, so the Nederburg Auction was born and first held in 1975; the Wine of Origin scheme is a law of origin, not a sale.

sources.title: Winemag: Nederburg Auction evolves into Cape Fine and Rare Wine Auction

report: The cellar master who made the first Edelkeur is reported living, aged 90 in 2024, by Wineland and two news pieces, so he is described and never named; the integrator may wish to add Gunter Brozel to people.json (the Wineland address carries his name, so that source may need replacing by the Citizen or Wine Economist piece if the lint is extended).

The German brewer who bought the farm in 1937 is named Johann Graue in Nederburg's own history and two secondary sources, but his dates of birth and death were not found in two sources (one gives his death as 1959), so he is described.

The making (cool ferment in steel, stopped, no wood), the grapes and the sites rest on the house's own Private Bin Edelkeur sheets for 2006, 2007, 2010 and 2012, read through search summaries of the house's hosted files; the Wine of Origin Western Cape is inferred from the 2012 sheet's blocks across the Western Cape and was not seen on a label, so the checker should confirm it.

The glass draws on IWSC notes of 2005, 2009 and 2010 (apricot, honey, melon, mango, dried fruit); marmalade, quince, wax and saffron are the author's reading of that profile and may be trimmed. The ageing line rests on the auction's sale of old vintages (Strauss and Co lots) rather than a stated window.
Eminence is told only as a Private Bin sweet wine, its grape not sourced.

The cap on residual sugar is 30 grams a litre on the house's history page and is left as a low level since only one source gives the figure; the 1972 second vintage rests on the Wine Economist and Wineland.
No swap proposed: Edelkeur is the house's founding wine for the auction and its sweet wine signature in every source read.

records.place: Paarl, at the KWV cellars in the town, Paarl district, Coastal Region

wine.name: The Mentors Perold
wine.grapes: A Cape Blend led by Pinotage, with Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon and smaller parts of Malbec or Cabernet Franc, in shares that move with the vintage.
wine.sites: Chosen vineyard blocks across the Coastal Region, Paarl among them, so the label carries the region rather than a single district.
wine.making: Each grape is fermented apart, and chosen wines of each go to barrel. After about twelve months in French oak a second selection of barrels is made and aged about six months more, some eighteen months in first fill French oak in all, before the blend is made and bottled.
wine.glass: Black plum, black cherry and mulled dark berries over clove, pepper and nutmeg, with tobacco and a smoky, tarry note from Pinotage; full and ripe, with fine, silky tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release for its fruit, it keeps and gains leather and tobacco for a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: KWV's own collection of small batch wines, which its pages call its flagship range.
The name of the scientist who crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut to make Pinotage.
Grapes from more than one district of the Coastal Region, Paarl and its neighbours.

records.table: KWV's The Mentors Perold is a Cape Blend led by Pinotage, with Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon, named for the scientist who made Pinotage and later worked for KWV. Eighteen months in French oak give plum, clove and silky tannin; decant it for an hour.
records.story: In 1918 the Cape's growers, battered by surplus after the First World War, formalised the Ko-operatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging at Paarl, with a board of twelve growers at its head. An act of 1924 gave the co-operative statutory duties and sole rights to export and import surplus wine and spirits, and for most of the century it set the terms of the trade. Abraham Izak Perold (1880 to 1941), the scientist who had crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut at Stellenbosch in the mid 1920s to make Pinotage, left the university to join KWV in 1928, where he trialled new grapes and raised the cellar's standards. In 1997, after almost eighty years as a co-operative, KWV converted itself into a company, and its role changed from regulating the industry to competing within it. The Mentors range followed as a collection of small batches chosen barrel by barrel, and Perold became its Cape Blend, a red in which Pinotage leads. It has since been a regular winner of the competition for Cape Blends, held in its namesake's honour. For a sommelier the wine joins the two threads of the house: the co-operative that shaped the Cape's trade and the man who gave the Cape its own grape.

others.name: The Mentors Orchestra
others.note: A Bordeaux style red blend of The Mentors range.

others.name: Roodeberg
others.note: The house's long standing red blend, the KWV red a guest is likeliest to have met.

others.name: KWV fortified wines and brandies
others.note: The Cape tawny and vintage styles and the potstill brandies the house is known for at home.

traps: Perold is a Cape Blend with Pinotage in the lead, not a varietal Pinotage; the grapes beside it move with the vintage.
The Mentors Perold carries Wine of Origin Coastal Region, not Paarl, though KWV's cellars stand in the town.
Pinotage was crossed by Perold at Stellenbosch University before he joined KWV in 1928; KWV did not create the grape.

cards.front: Who is The Mentors Perold of KWV named for, and what did he make?
cards.back: Abraham Izak Perold (1880 to 1941), who crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut to make Pinotage.
It converted from a co-operative into a company, after almost eighty years.

A varietal Pinotage from one Paarl vineyard

A fortified red in the Cape tawny style
questions.exp: Perold is a Cape Blend in which Pinotage leads, with Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and smaller parts; The Mentors Orchestra is the house's Bordeaux style blend.

questions.q: What powers did the act of 1924 give KWV?
opts: Statutory duties and sole rights over surplus exports
The right to grant Wine of Origin seals
Ownership of every cellar in Paarl
Control of the Nederburg Auction
questions.exp: The KWV Act of 1924 gave the co-operative statutory duties and sole rights to export and import surplus alcohol; the Wine of Origin scheme came in 1973 under another law.

report: Charles Kohler, the co-operative's driving force and first chairman, is left unnamed since his dates were not read in two sources (sahistory.org.za holds a page on him); the checker may name him with dates from two sources.

The founding is 1918 by KWV and Wikipedia (registered December 1917, formalised 8 January 1918); the conversion to a company in 1997 rests on KWV's timeline and the Mail and Guardian report of December 1997.

Perold's dates (20 October 1880 to 11 December 1941) are in Wikipedia and the Pinotage Association's page; he joined KWV in 1928 by KWV's own history and Wikipedia, with one source giving 1927. The crossing is told as the mid 1920s since sources give 1924 and 1925.

The making (twelve months, a second selection, about six months more, eighteen months in first fill French oak) rests on KWV's sheets for 2020 and 2021 and Wineland's Veritas reports; the Wine of Origin Coastal Region is on both KWV sheets, Decanter and Jancis Robinson.

The blend rests on Concours and Wineland listings for 2021 and 2022 (Pinotage, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec) and Jim's Cellars (with Cabernet Franc); the glass on IWC notes of 2017, 2019 and 2022 and Concours of 2021; the ageing on Gilbert and Gaillard's window for 2021.

The first vintage of Perold and the launch year of The Mentors were not found in two sources and are left out; the competition for Cape Blends is told without a count of wins. Roodeberg's founding year is left out.
No swap proposed.

records.place: The south western slopes of Paarl Mountain, Paarl district, Coastal Region

wine.name: Cyril Back
wine.grapes: Shiraz, all of it in some vintages, with a smaller part of Cabernet Sauvignon in others; the house lets the wine be any grape the year favours.
wine.sites: Dry farmed vineyards, bush vines among them, in Agter-Paarl and the Swartland in the vintages read, so the label carries the Coastal Region rather than Paarl.
wine.making: Chosen barrels of the year's Shiraz go into it. In the vintages read it spent a long time in French oak, from about two years to two and a half, much of it new, and it was bottled unfined and only lightly filtered.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and plum over black pepper, anise and violet, with cigar box and nutmeg from the oak; dense and ripe, with firm, polished tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and oaky in youth, it wants five years or more and will keep for well over a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the founder's son, who ran the farm from 1955 and began its own label.
Grapes drawn from more than one district, Paarl and the Swartland in the vintages read.

records.table: Cyril Back is Fairview's flagship red, named for the man who first bottled wine under the farm's own label: Shiraz led, from dry farmed vines in Agter-Paarl and the Swartland, aged long in French oak. It is dense and peppery, so decant it.
records.story: The family's founder at the Cape bought Fairview, on the slopes of Paarl Mountain, in 1937. When he died in 1955 he left the farm to his son, for whom the flagship is named, who farmed it and, like most Cape growers of his day, delivered his wine to the KWV. In 1974 the son broke with that habit and bottled the first wines under the Fairview label, from grapes grown only on the farm, a Cabernet Sauvignon, a Shiraz and a Pinotage among them. In 1980 the family began the herd of dairy goats that gave the farm its cheese and, in time, the jokes on its labels. The founder's grandson joined the family company in 1978 and took it over in 1995, on his father's death, and the house widened its range across the Rhône grapes and towards the Swartland, where its vines grow on dry land. The flagship red took his father's name, and the house allows it to be any grape the vintage favours, though in the vintages read it has been Shiraz, alone or with a little Cabernet Sauvignon. For a sommelier the wine marks the year 1974, when a Paarl farm stopped selling to the co-operative and began to speak in its own name.

others.name: Caldera
others.note: The house's Rhône style red blend of Grenache, Shiraz and Mourvèdre.

others.name: Goats do Roam
others.note: The playful Rhône style range whose name puns on the Côtes du Rhône, born of the farm's goats.

others.name: Beryl Back
others.note: A Wine of Origin Paarl red named for another of the family.

traps: Cyril Back is not a fixed varietal: it has been pure Shiraz in some years and Shiraz with Cabernet Sauvignon in others.
Fairview's flagship carries Wine of Origin Coastal Region, since its fruit has come from Agter-Paarl and the Swartland, not Paarl Mountain alone.
Fairview and Backsberg are different houses, though both were founded by the same family and split between brothers in 1955.

cards.back: It bottled wine under its own label instead of delivering it to the KWV.

cards.front: Fairview's Cyril Back: where did the fruit come from in the vintages read?
cards.back: Dry farmed vineyards in Agter-Paarl and the Swartland.

opts: Shiraz leads, sometimes with a little Cabernet
Pinotage alone, from Paarl Mountain
A Rhône blend of Grenache and Mourvèdre
Cabernet Franc and Merlot in equal parts

questions.q: When the family's founder died in 1955, how were his farms divided?
opts: Fairview to one son, Backsberg to the other
Both farms sold to the KWV
Fairview given to a co-operative of Paarl growers
Both farms left to his grandson
questions.exp: He left Fairview to the son the flagship is named for and Backsberg to his brother; the grandson joined the company only in 1978.

report: Cyril Back is named only as the wine and its label; in prose he is the founder's son, since his dates were not found in two sources (his death in 1995 rests on Wikipedia's page on his son alone). The founder and his grandson share a name with a living person in people.json and are never named.

The purchase of 1937, the death of 1955 and the division of Fairview and Backsberg rest on Wikipedia and South African History Online; the first own label wines of 1974 on the same two and the house's family page.

The blend and making rest on the house's sheets for 2013 (all Shiraz, 26 months in new French oak) and 2014 (Shiraz with some Cabernet, unfined and lightly filtered) and on listings for 2017, 2018 and 2022 (19 to 30 months in French oak); the Wine of Origin Coastal Region rests on Cape Ardor's listings and the Agter-Paarl and Swartland fruit of the 2013 sheet, and was not seen on a label.

The glass rests on the house's notes for 2013 and 2016 (blueberry, plum, anise, nutmeg, blackberry, pepper, violet, cigar box) and Cape Ardor's for 2022; the ageing is the author's reading of the house's own claim to age well.

The first vintage of Cyril Back is not known from any source read and is left out; Beryl Back is named only from its Wine of Origin Paarl sheet, and whom it honours is left unsaid. The goat herd of 1980 rests on the house's timeline.

records.place: Northern foothills of the Simonsberg, Simonsberg-Paarl ward, Paarl district

wine.name: Quartz Stone Chardonnay
wine.sites: By the house's account its oldest Chardonnay block, planted in 1989 on the northern foothills of the Simonsberg, on decomposed granite with much quartz in it, which gives the wine its name; from 2024 the house also drew on chosen blocks beyond it.
wine.making: Picked and sorted by hand and pressed in whole bunches, using only the first, gentlest free run juice. It ferments with its own yeasts, without malolactic fermentation, and ages on its gross lees for about twelve months, mostly in new French oak barriques with a small part in a concrete egg, before a selection of barrels is bottled.
wine.glass: Preserved lemon, quince and white peach over toasted hazelnut, ginger and a flinty, smoky edge; taut and bright rather than buttery, with lively acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and oaky in its first two or three years, it gains hazelnut and honey and keeps well for eight to ten years.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The block's soil of decomposed granite strewn with quartz.
The ward on the northern slopes of the Simonsberg, within the Paarl district.

records.table: Glen Carlou's Quartz Stone Chardonnay comes from the block the house calls its oldest Chardonnay, planted in 1989 on quartz strewn granite below the Simonsberg. Wild fermented, with no malolactic, and aged a year in mostly new French oak, it is taut, lemony and nutty.
records.story: The farm on the northern foothills of the Simonsberg, once called Lencarlou, was bought in 1985 by a winemaker of Scottish descent, who renamed it Glen Carlou for his ancestry; vines had gone in the year before, under a partnership. By the house's own account it has built its name since 1988 on Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon, and it counts itself among the first producers of Chardonnay at the Cape, at a time when the grape was rare there. In 1989 it planted the block that would become Quartz Stone, on decomposed granite full of quartz. In 2003 the wine group of the Swiss Hess family bought the estate from the founding family. In 2016 a South African family consortium took it over. With the 2024 vintage the house began to draw Quartz Stone from chosen Chardonnay blocks beyond the old one, so it is no longer a single block wine. For a sommelier Quartz Stone shows the cooler, granite face of Paarl: a district known for warmth and Shiraz also gives Chardonnay of tension.

others.name: Gravel Quarry Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The house's other single site wine, a Cabernet Sauvignon from gravel rich ground, the pair of Quartz Stone.

others.name: Glen Carlou Chardonnay
others.note: The estate Chardonnay, the house's wider bottling of the grape it built its name on.

traps: Quartz Stone carries Wine of Origin Simonsberg-Paarl, a ward of Paarl, not Simonsberg-Stellenbosch on the mountain's other side.
From 2024 Quartz Stone draws on several chosen blocks, so earlier bottles from the single block of 1989 and later ones differ.
Quartz Stone is made without malolactic fermentation, so it is taut and citric, not buttery, despite its new oak.

Ageing in old American oak
Picking late for extra ripeness

questions.exp: Quartz Stone does not go through malolactic fermentation, which keeps its acidity bright; new French oak gives it nuttiness but not butter.

report: The founders are not known to be dead and are not named; the founder's Scottish ancestry and the renaming rest on Wein.plus and a second wiki style page, the partnership and vines of 1984 on one search summary only, which the checker may wish to cut.

The Hess purchase of 2003 rests on two secondary sources; one wiki gives a half share in 1995 first, unconfirmed and left out. The consortium of 2016 rests on the house's own heritage page and Wein.plus; no name of the consortium's leader is given, as he is living.

The block of 1989, the making (whole bunch, first free run juice, own yeasts, no malolactic, twelve months on gross lees, mostly new French oak with a concrete egg) and the change of 2024 rest on the house's sheets for 2023 and 2024; the house's sheet gives about ninety per cent new oak.
The first vintage of Quartz Stone was not found in any source and is left out. The Hess group's other wineries and the estate's art gallery were not sourced and are left out.

The glass rests on notes for 2021 and 2024 (preserved lemon, quince, hazelnut, candied lemon, ginger, smoke) and Fairleys (white peach, buttered toast); the ageing is the author's reading and may be trimmed.

records.place: The foot of the Paardeberg, Agter-Paarl, Paarl district, Coastal Region

wine.name: The Dry Land Collection Courageous Barrel Fermented Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: An old, unirrigated Chenin Blanc vineyard planted in 1985 in the Paarl area and certified by the Old Vine Project as a heritage vineyard.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed and left on their skins for about two hours, then fermented and aged for ten to eleven months in 500 litre French oak barrels, most of them used and a fifth or so new, on the lees without stirring and without malolactic fermentation, and aged some months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, yellow peach and pineapple over lemon, lychee and a touch of vanilla from the barrel; rich and broad in the middle, with a crisp line of Chenin acidity and a clean, honeyed finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it holds and gains honey and nut for five to eight years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's range from unirrigated vineyards only, first released in 2013.
One of the range's names, each standing for a trait of its vineyard.
Fermented and aged in oak barrels, here 500 litre French casks.

records.table: Perdeberg's Courageous is the barrel fermented Chenin Blanc of its Dry Land Collection, from unirrigated vines planted in 1985 near the Paardeberg. Ten months in large French barrels give it pear, peach and vanilla over a crisp line of acidity.
records.story: In 1941 a grower at the foot of the Paardeberg, unhappy with what their grapes earned, gathered the district's farmers to make wine of their own rather than sell their fruit, and the cellar pressed its first grapes by hand in 1942. Its name recalls the mountain zebra that once roamed the foothills, which early Dutch settlers took for wild horses. The cellar grew as a co-operative on the dry farmed bush vines of Agter-Paarl and the Swartland's edge, and it came to call itself the home of Chenin Blanc. In 2013 it launched The Dry Land Collection, made only from unirrigated vineyards, each wine named for a trait of its site, and its first vintage won the cellar a producer's title at the Michelangelo awards of 2014. The Courageous, its barrel fermented Chenin from a vineyard planted in 1985, became the range's white of most weight, a regular in the Cape's Chenin competitions, and it was later certified as a heritage vineyard. In 2021, for its eightieth year, the cellar made Rex Equus, a red blend in a limited bottling. For a sommelier Courageous is the voice of a growers' cellar: old Paarl Chenin, grown without water, made with care in oak.

others.name: Rex Equus
others.note: The red blend of Bordeaux grapes made for the cellar's eightieth year in 2021, in a limited numbered bottling.

others.name: The Dry Land Collection Chenin Blanc
others.note: The range's unoaked Chenin, a lighter companion of the Courageous.

traps: Perdeberg lies in Agter-Paarl at the foot of the Paardeberg; it is not the Perdeberg of Stellenbosch, and its Courageous carries Wine of Origin Paarl, not Swartland.
The Courageous is oaked in large 500 litre barrels, mostly used, and made without malolactic fermentation, so it keeps its freshness under the oak.
Rex Equus is an anniversary red of 2021, not the head of a standing range.

cards.front: What do the wines of Perdeberg's Dry Land Collection share?
cards.back: They come only from unirrigated vineyards, and each name stands for a trait of its site.

cards.front: When did Perdeberg begin, and when did it press its first grapes?
cards.back: Founded in 1941 by growers who wanted to make their own wine; first grapes pressed by hand in 1942.

In small new American oak barrels
In stainless steel with no oak
In clay amphorae buried in the ground

questions.q: Why did the growers of the Paardeberg found Perdeberg in 1941?
opts: To make their own wine instead of selling grapes
To supply grapes to Nederburg's new auction
To plant the Cape's first Chenin Blanc
To bottle wine for the KWV's export trade

Perdeberg Wines: Perdeberg's Dry Land Collection
Falstaff: Perdeberg Cellar 2024 Courageous Barrel Fermented Chenin Blanc

report: Thin region rule: Perdeberg is a growers' cellar known at home far more than abroad, and no source names a single flagship; the Courageous is chosen as the Chenin the cellar enters in competitions and sets in its ultra premium shop range, and the story says what the house is.

The founding of 1941, the first pressing of 1942, the zebra name and the Dry Land Collection of 2013 rest on the house's own pages, with 1941 also in winetourism.com and others. The founder, named Jan Rossouw by the house, is described since his dates were not found.
When the co-operative became a company was not found in any source and is left out; a trade listing calls it a former co-operative. No size or volume claim is made.
